props.title: Stavisky
props.initialSlug: French con man's lavish rise and fatal downfall

sections.content: Alain Resnais's **Stavisky (1974)** (1974) brilliantly captures the glittering facade of 1930s French society through the true story of con man Alexandre Stavisky. Jean-Paul Belmondo delivers one of his most nuanced performances as the charming swindler who infiltrated France's upper echelons. Like **The Great Gatsby** (1974), released the same year, it explores wealth, deception and the dark underbelly of excessive glamour. Resnais employs his signature non-linear storytelling, jumping between Stavisky's rise and fall while Stephen Sondheim's lush score amplifies the period's decadent atmosphere. movies.title: Stavisky
movies.slug: Alain Resnais directs Jean-Paul Belmondo in this stylish drama about a real-life French financial fraudster in the 1930s

sections.content: The film exemplifies a fascinating moment in 1970s European cinema when directors turned to examining pre-WWII society with both nostalgia and critique. Like Visconti's **The Garden of the Finzi-Continis** (1970) and Bertolucci's The Conformist (1970), **Stavisky** depicts the elegant but morally bankrupt world that would soon face fascism's rise. Resnais's approach differs in focusing on financial rather than political corruption, though the film suggests how the Stavisky Affair contributed to France's political instability. SUBHEAD: Style and Historical Context

Resnais's sophisticated visual style reaches new heights here, with cinematographer Sacha Vierny creating a golden-hued world of art deco interiors and winter resorts. The approach influenced later period films like **Death in Venice** (1971) and **The Last Metro** (1980), showing how meticulous production design could serve both historical accuracy and thematic resonance. The film's examination of financial fraud and social pretense also anticipates later works like **The Wolf of Wall Street** (2013) and **Catch Me If You Can** (2002).
